title: Zero of Eight: Why Typing Broke Grammar Practice | vitalii.no
description:
My son typed grammar answers on a phone keyboard, and on 27 August he got zero out of eight right in one sitting. Three of those attempts had the correct word, killed by a single stray typo. After that he gave up and started typing junk like 'Hhh' and 'Cvh'. A keyboard on a phone was punishing his spelling, not testing his grammar.

I pulled every text field out of the language exercises and replaced it with a tap-based syllable and word builder. A word is cut into syllables, a short answer is cut into words, and the bank of tappable chunks is shuffled per answer with decoy chunks mixed in — a thumb slip can no longer spell a wrong word into being. Grammar itself now turns each sentence-and-correction pair into tap-the-word, tap-to-remove, tap-the-slot, or rebuild-the-sentence exercises, depending on exactly what changed. For older sentences that never had a saved correct answer, a recovery routine pulls the correction straight out of the existing explanation text.

That recovery routine reclaimed a usable answer for seventeen of the thirty live sentences that had none — the other thirteen correctly declined rather than risk a guessed exercise. Reading, English recall, and grammar all now run through the same tap mechanism instead of a phone keyboard.
